repositories.meaning: The total number of configured repositories across local, remote, virtual, and federated types.
repositories.why: A large repository estate increases the need for ownership, lifecycle, and access governance.

repositories-total.meaning: The total number of configured repositories in this report scope.
repositories-total.why: This shows the size of the package-management estate the platform supports.

local-repositories.meaning: Repositories that store packages produced or retained by your organization.
local-repositories.why: Local repositories are the governed system of record for internally owned software assets.

remote-repositories.meaning: Configured proxies for external package sources.
remote-repositories.why: Remote repositories reduce direct internet access and provide a controlled cache for third-party dependencies.

virtual-repositories.meaning: Stable endpoints that combine multiple repositories behind one developer-facing URL.
virtual-repositories.why: Virtual repositories simplify developer setup and centralize policy enforcement.

federated-repositories.meaning: Repositories synchronized across participating JFrog locations.
federated-repositories.why: Federation supports multi-site availability but adds replication and governance considerations.

artifacts-total.meaning: The number of artifact records stored in the selected scope.
artifacts-total.why: Artifact volume is an indicator of platform adoption and lifecycle-management demand.

artifacts-count.meaning: The number of stored files represented by the Artifactory storage summary.
artifacts-count.why: This helps explain storage growth and the operational scale managed by Artifactory.

storage-tib.meaning: The physical storage used by artifacts in this report scope.
storage-tib.why: Storage trend is a core input to capacity planning and cost governance.

artifact-storage.meaning: The physical storage consumed by artifacts at the time of collection.
artifact-storage.why: This is a capacity baseline; period growth requires comparison with an earlier snapshot.

binary-dedup-optimization.meaning: The estimated storage avoided because identical binary content is stored once and referenced many times.
binary-dedup-optimization.why: This indicates infrastructure efficiency, but is not a cash saving unless avoided capacity has a supplied cost.

empty-repositories.meaning: Configured repositories that currently contain no stored files in the storage summary.
empty-repositories.why: They may be intentional, new, or candidates for ownership and cleanup review.

projects-with-storage.meaning: JFrog Projects that own repositories with stored content.
projects-with-storage.why: Project attribution makes ownership, showback, and delegated administration easier.

period-downloads.meaning: Successful artifact downloads during the report period when a bounded metric or log source is connected.
period-downloads.why: Download trend measures adoption and helps capacity planning; a current storage snapshot cannot reconstruct it.

period-uploads.meaning: Successful artifact uploads during the report period when a bounded metric or log source is connected.
period-uploads.why: Upload trend reflects software production and publishing activity; artifact creation timestamps are not a complete substitute.

binary-cache-hit-rate.meaning: The share of binary-provider lookups served from cache, calculated from same-period Open Metrics counter deltas.
binary-cache-hit-rate.why: Cache efficiency can reduce latency and upstream load, but it is not the same as remote-repository dependency reuse.

downloads.meaning: Artifact download activity during the selected period, when a period-capable source is available.
downloads.why: Download volume is an adoption signal and an input to transfer and cache-efficiency analysis.

access-long-lived.meaning: Active tokens whose configured expiry is more than 90 days after the snapshot time.
access-long-lived.why: Long-lived credentials retain access for an extended period and should have an explicit owner and rotation justification.

builds-published.meaning: Build records published during the selected period.
builds-published.why: Build-info adoption improves traceability from source and CI to released artifacts.

curation-decisions.meaning: Package requests evaluated by Curation during the report period.
curation-decisions.why: This shows how much third-party dependency activity passed through preventive policy controls.

curation-approved.meaning: Package requests allowed after Curation evaluated them.
curation-approved.why: Approved traffic shows policy governing dependency use without treating every request as risky.

curation-blocked.meaning: Package requests stopped by an active Curation policy.
curation-blocked.why: A block is a prevented policy violation, not automatically a prevented breach or cash saving.

curation-blocks.meaning: Package requests stopped by Curation in the selected period.
curation-blocks.why: This is the clearest observed measure of preventive control activity.

curation-block-rate.meaning: The share of evaluated package requests that Curation blocked.
curation-block-rate.why: This separates broad developer activity from the smaller portion that triggered policy.

curation-users.meaning: Distinct requester identities seen in Curation decisions; identities can include people, service users, or tokens.
curation-users.why: This is an adoption indicator, not a licensed-seat count.

active-curation-users.meaning: Distinct requester identities that generated Curation activity during the period.
active-curation-users.why: This shows how broadly preventive dependency controls are being exercised.

curation-users-approved.meaning: Requester identities with at least one package request approved by Curation.
curation-users-approved.why: This indicates active, policy-governed consumption rather than only blocked traffic.

curation-repos.meaning: Repositories represented in Curation decisions during the period.
curation-repos.why: This indicates how broadly Curation protection is used across package entry points.

unique-blocked-packages.meaning: Distinct package-and-version combinations stopped by Curation.
unique-blocked-packages.why: This separates risky dependency breadth from repeat attempts for the same dependency.

unique-blocked.meaning: Distinct package versions stopped by Curation during the period.
unique-blocked.why: This is a better measure of blocked dependency breadth than raw request count alone.

curation-repeat-block-attempts.meaning: Blocked requests beyond the first block for each package version.
curation-repeat-block-attempts.why: Repeat attempts can indicate unresolved demand, automation retries, or a need for clearer alternatives.

curation-blocks-per-user.meaning: Average blocked requests per active requester identity.
curation-blocks-per-user.why: This normalizes preventive activity for the size of the active population.

curation-active-blocking-policies.meaning: Enabled policies that stop a request when their conditions match.
curation-active-blocking-policies.why: This is the policy inventory with direct preventive effect.

curation-active-dry-run-policies.meaning: Enabled policies that record matches but do not stop the request.
curation-active-dry-run-policies.why: Dry-run policies show controls still being evaluated before enforcement.

curation-cache-enforcing-policies.meaning: Blocking policies that also stop disallowed packages already present in a remote cache.
curation-cache-enforcing-policies.why: Without cache enforcement, a package cached before policy activation may remain consumable.

curation-cache-gap-policies.meaning: Blocking policies that do not apply their decision to packages already in cache.
curation-cache-gap-policies.why: These policies may leave a gap between new external requests and previously cached packages.

xray-indexed.meaning: Repositories configured for Xray indexing and scanning.
xray-indexed.why: Only indexed repositories receive the configured Xray analysis and policy evaluation.

xray-non-indexed.meaning: Repositories not configured for Xray indexing.
xray-non-indexed.why: Their content may sit outside the intended security and license-control coverage.

xray-index-coverage.meaning: The percentage of eligible repositories configured for Xray indexing.
xray-index-coverage.why: Coverage shows whether findings describe most of the estate or only a subset.

xray-watches.meaning: Configured Xray watches that connect resources to security policies.
xray-watches.why: Watches define where policy is applied; count alone does not prove effective coverage.

xray-active-watches.meaning: Xray watches currently enabled for evaluation.
xray-active-watches.why: Inactive watches do not produce ongoing policy evaluation.

xray-covered-resources.meaning: Resources explicitly named by active Xray watches.
xray-covered-resources.why: This helps explain the practical scope of configured security policy.

xray-policies.meaning: Configured Xray security and license policies.
xray-policies.why: Assignment and enforcement state determine whether a configured policy has practical effect.

xray-unassigned-policies.meaning: Policies not connected to an active watch.
xray-unassigned-policies.why: An unassigned policy is configured but not actively governing a watched resource.

xray-new-findings.meaning: New violation occurrences created during the report period after cross-watch deduplication.
xray-new-findings.why: This measures period intake, not the total unresolved vulnerability backlog.

xray-critical-findings.meaning: New period violation occurrences classified as Critical.
xray-critical-findings.why: Critical intake deserves rapid triage, but exploitability and runtime context still matter.

xray-critical-period.meaning: Critical Xray violation activity newly observed during the selected period.
xray-critical-period.why: This highlights the most severe new security-policy intake for executive attention.

xray-unique-cves.meaning: Distinct CVE identifiers represented in new period violations.
xray-unique-cves.why: This separates vulnerability variety from repeated occurrences across many artifacts.

xray-affected-artifacts.meaning: Distinct artifact paths associated with new period violations.
xray-affected-artifacts.why: This approximates technical remediation scope, not the number of deployed applications affected.

xray-fix-available.meaning: New violation occurrences for which Xray reported at least one fix version.
xray-fix-available.why: Fix availability helps teams prioritize work with a known upgrade path.

jas-policies.meaning: Security policies configured with at least one JFrog Advanced Security criterion.
jas-policies.why: This proves configuration, not that every JAS scanner ran or produced findings.

jas-watch-assignments.meaning: Active watch assignments that apply policies containing JAS criteria.
jas-watch-assignments.why: Assignments show where advanced controls are intended to operate.

jas-configured-resources.meaning: Resources named by watches that use JAS-enabled policies.
jas-configured-resources.why: This is configuration coverage and should not be read as confirmed scan coverage.

jas-capabilities.meaning: Distinct JAS control types found in configured policies.
jas-capabilities.why: This shows the breadth of advanced security capabilities configured in policy.

jas-applicable.meaning: Findings whose vulnerable code path was confirmed applicable by contextual analysis.
jas-applicable.why: Applicable findings are stronger remediation candidates than vulnerabilities present but unreachable.

jas-applicable-period.meaning: Period findings confirmed applicable by JAS contextual analysis.
jas-applicable-period.why: This focuses attention on vulnerabilities with stronger evidence of real application exposure.

jas-not-applicable.meaning: Findings analyzed and determined not applicable in the inspected context.
jas-not-applicable.why: This can reduce remediation noise while preserving the underlying vulnerability evidence.

jas-rescan-required.meaning: Findings whose applicability result requires another scan before a current conclusion can be made.
jas-rescan-required.why: They should not be treated as safe or applicable until analysis is refreshed.

jas-not-scanned.meaning: Findings without a completed applicability analysis.
jas-not-scanned.why: They remain unprioritized and must not be counted as not applicable.

ai-repositories-total.meaning: Repositories whose package type is associated with AI models, agent skills, plugins, or related assets.
ai-repositories-total.why: This shows governed Artifactory footprint; it does not prove use or AI Catalog approval.

ai-repositories-active.meaning: AI- or agent-related repositories that store at least one file.
ai-repositories-active.why: This distinguishes configured capacity from repositories with actual content.

ai-stored-items.meaning: Files stored in the identified AI- and agent-related repositories.
ai-stored-items.why: This is not a count of unique models, skills, MCP servers, or active consumers.

ai-storage-gib.meaning: Storage consumed by the identified AI- and agent-related repositories.
ai-storage-gib.why: This supports capacity and ownership review without claiming security posture or adoption.

ai-projects.meaning: JFrog Projects with stored content in AI- or agent-related repositories.
ai-projects.why: This indicates organizational spread and helps route ownership and governance conversations.

ai-detected-models.meaning: Models detected across the governed environment at collection time.
ai-detected-models.why: This is the baseline used to identify model adoption and governance gaps.

ai-allowed-models.meaning: Models explicitly allowed in the AI Catalog, across package, external, and custom types.
ai-allowed-models.why: Allowed inventory shows the approved model choices available to projects.

ai-allowed-mcp-servers.meaning: MCP servers explicitly allowed through the AI Catalog registry.
ai-allowed-mcp-servers.why: A governed MCP inventory reduces unmanaged agent access to tools and data.

ai-registered-skills.meaning: Versioned agent skills registered in the AI Catalog.
ai-registered-skills.why: Central registration improves discovery, reuse, ownership, and version traceability.

ai-scanned-skills.meaning: Registered skills whose AI/Xray security scan reached a completed state.
ai-scanned-skills.why: The difference between registered and scanned skills exposes a governance coverage gap.

ai-registered-plugins.meaning: Versioned agent plugins registered in the AI Catalog.
ai-registered-plugins.why: Plugins can bundle powerful agent capabilities and need the same ownership and release controls as software packages.

ai-shadow-models.meaning: Model packages detected in repositories but not yet governed by the AI Catalog.
ai-shadow-models.why: Shadow models reveal AI use that has not completed approval or dismissal.

ai-shadow-managed.meaning: Detected model packages already brought under AI Catalog governance.
ai-shadow-managed.why: This shows how much discovered AI use has an explicit management decision.

ai-shadow-unmanaged.meaning: Detected model packages that remain outside AI Catalog governance.
ai-shadow-unmanaged.why: These models need an allow, block, or dismiss decision so shadow adoption does not remain invisible.

ai-live-models.meaning: Models with current AI gateway activity in the collected window.
ai-live-models.why: This separates approved inventory from models teams are actively using.

ai-gateway-requests.meaning: Requests sent through the governed AI gateway during the bounded collection period.
ai-gateway-requests.why: Gateway activity provides an adoption trend without treating catalog presence as consumption.

ai-visible-skills.meaning: Skill rows visible in the supplied AI Catalog registry capture; this is not asserted as the complete catalog total.
ai-visible-skills.why: It proves skill registry adoption while avoiding a false total when the captured table is scrollable.

ai-not-malicious-skills.meaning: Visible skills whose latest version returned the completed JFrog Xray status Not malicious.
ai-not-malicious-skills.why: This shows how much of the visible skill inventory completed security evaluation without a malicious classification.

ai-malicious-skills.meaning: Visible skills whose latest version returned a malicious JFrog Xray classification.
ai-malicious-skills.why: Any non-zero result requires immediate containment and investigation before the skill is used.

ai-unscanned-skills.meaning: Visible skills whose latest version has not completed a JFrog Xray skill scan.
ai-unscanned-skills.why: Unscanned skills create a governance gap and should not be confused with skills found safe.

ai-scanning-skills.meaning: Visible skills whose latest version was still being scanned at collection time.
ai-scanning-skills.why: These are pending decisions, not clean results, and should be checked again after processing completes.

ai-suspicious-skills.meaning: Visible skills whose latest version returned a suspicious JFrog Xray classification.
ai-suspicious-skills.why: Suspicious skills need review before approval because the scan found signals that warrant investigation.

access-active-tokens.meaning: Access-token records returned by the active token inventory at collection time.
access-active-tokens.why: Token volume establishes the credential-governance workload; it does not include already purged historical tokens.

access-new-tokens-30d.meaning: Active tokens issued during the 30 days before collection.
access-new-tokens-30d.why: Issuance velocity can reveal automation growth or unexpected credential churn.

access-expiring-7d.meaning: Active tokens whose configured expiry falls within seven days of collection.
access-expiring-7d.why: These credentials need immediate rotation or retirement planning to avoid outages.

access-expiring-30d.meaning: Active tokens whose configured expiry falls within 30 days of collection.
access-expiring-30d.why: This is the near-term credential rotation workload.

access-non-expiring.meaning: Active token records without a configured expiry timestamp.
access-non-expiring.why: Non-expiring credentials increase persistence and should have explicit ownership and compensating controls.

access-never-used.meaning: Active tokens for which Access returned no last-used timestamp.
access-never-used.why: Unused credentials may be candidates for verification and revocation, reducing attack surface.

oidc-providers.meaning: Configured OIDC trust providers used for external identity and workload authentication.
oidc-providers.why: OIDC reduces reliance on stored long-lived CI/CD secrets.

oidc-mappings.meaning: Configured identity mappings that translate external OIDC claims into JFrog token scope.
oidc-mappings.why: Mapping review verifies that repository and workflow trust remains appropriately scoped.

oidc-repository-patterns.meaning: OIDC mapping claims that name an exact repository or repository pattern.
oidc-repository-patterns.why: Broad wildcard patterns deserve review because they can authorize more source repositories than an exact mapping.

runtime-critical-high.meaning: Critical and high vulnerabilities associated with production images monitored by Runtime.
runtime-critical-high.why: This is the broad production-risk funnel before runtime applicability narrows the response queue.

runtime-applicable.meaning: Production findings whose vulnerable code was found applicable in the running context.
runtime-applicable.why: Applicability focuses remediation on risks with stronger evidence of real exposure.

runtime-fix-available.meaning: Applicable production findings for which a fixed version is available.
runtime-fix-available.why: These are high-value remediation candidates because an upgrade path is known.

runtime-validated.meaning: Findings further validated by Runtime observation in production.
runtime-validated.why: Runtime validation is stronger prioritization evidence than package presence alone.

runtime-images.meaning: Running image tags assessed by Runtime Security at collection time.
runtime-images.why: This establishes the production population behind the risk counts.

runtime-malicious-packages.meaning: Malicious packages identified in currently running images.
runtime-malicious-packages.why: Any non-zero result warrants immediate incident triage and containment.

runtime-critical-applicable.meaning: Critical vulnerabilities confirmed applicable in running images.
runtime-critical-applicable.why: This is a compact executive view of the most actionable production vulnerability risk.

runtime-integrity-violations.meaning: Running images with evidence of drift or integrity-policy violation.
runtime-integrity-violations.why: Integrity violations can indicate unapproved change or tampering after release.
